steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Lumiere, a Byzantine view synchronization protocol for state machine replication under partial synchrony. Motivate the view synchronization problem, state the complexity and latency goals, compare with prior protocols, state the main theorem, and sketch the technical approach.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. SMR and the push for efficiency at scale
2. Byzantine fault tolerance and the partial synchrony model
3. View-based paradigm and the BVS problem
4. HotStuff and why view synchronization is the bottleneck
5. Desired complexity, latency and responsiveness properties
6. Prior work and the main result (Theorem 1.1)
7. Technical approach: combining LP22 and Fever; epoch-change elimination

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. SMR
- central topic in distributed computing; fault-tolerant service by replicating servers, coordinating clients with replicas
- 'blockchain' investment -> interest in SMR protocols efficient at scale
- minimize latency and communication complexity per consensus decision as a function of n processors

2. BFT and partial synchrony
- consensus even if bounded proportion Byzantine (arbitrary/malicious)
- partial synchrony model: common, compromise between synchronous and asynchronous
- GST: message sent at time t arrives by \max\{\text{GST},t\}+\Delta; \Delta known, GST unknown
- optimal resiliency: up to f Byzantine among n, f largest integer less than n/3

3. View-based paradigm
- many BFT SMR protocols use views, each with designated leader
- decision guaranteed during synchrony when honest processors spend long enough in a view with honest leader
- ensuring this = Byzantine View Synchronization (BVS) problem

4. HotStuff
- first to decouple core consensus logic from "Pacemaker" module implementing BVS; pacemaker left unspecified
- core logic: quadratic worst-case communication, linear latency; each view linear complexity, constant rounds
- view synchronization = efficiency bottleneck
- key question: BVS protocol with optimal communication complexity and latency?

5. Requirements
- worst-case complexity O(n^{2}) (Dolev-Reischuk bound)
- with fewer actual faults f_{a}\leq f: complexity between decisions o(n^{2}) when f_{a}=o(n)
- worst-case latency O(n\Delta); hope for o(n\Delta) with few faults
- optimistic responsiveness: 'network speed' if f_{a}=0; latency a function of actual delay \delta
- \delta may be much smaller than conservatively set \Delta
- formal: after GST, latency between synchronized honest-leader views O(\delta) when f_{a}=0
- smoothly optimistically responsive: O(\Delta f_{a}+\delta) for any f_{a}\leq f

6. Prior work and result
- recent works achieve some goals
- shortcomings: only benign failures; not optimal worst-case; large cost even with few faults; clock synchronization
- Lumiere first BVS protocol in partial synchrony with all properties
- Theorem: (1) O(n^{2}) worst-case communication, (2) O(n\Delta) worst-case latency, (3) smoothly optimistically responsive, (4) eventual worst case communication O(f_{a}n+n)
- terms defined in Section 2; Table 1 comparison; details in Section 6

7. Approach
- first to satisfy (1) and (2) plus (3) or (4) (in fact both)
- combine LP22 and Fever
- LP22: epochs of f+1 views; heavy (\Theta(n^{2})) synchronization only at start of each epoch -> matches Dolev-Reischuk; optimistically responsive but one faulty leader -> \Theta(n\Delta) delays
- Fever: optimal for all measures but needs synchronized clocks (non-standard model)
- epochs as in LP22 + Fever within epochs -> (1)–(3)
- hardest part: property (4), stop heavy epoch changes once sufficiently synchronized; Section 3.5

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
State machine replication (SMR) is a central topic in distributed computing. It refers to the task of implementing a fault-tolerant service by replicating servers and coordinating the interactions of clients with the server replicas. Partly because of high levels of investment in ‘blockchain’ technology, in recent years there has been interest in developing SMR protocols that work efficiently at scale. Concretely, this means trying to minimize the latency and the communication complexity per consensus decision as a function of the number of processors (participants) n.

SMR protocols usually aim for Byzantine fault tolerance, which means consensus among the processors (server replicas) even if a bounded proportion of them are Byzantine and behave arbitrarily/maliciously. Many of these protocols are based on the partial synchrony model, which is a common networking model and can be seen as a practical compromise between the synchronous and asynchronous communication models. The model assumes a point in time called the global stabilisation time (GST) so that any message sent at time t has to arrive by time \max\{\text{GST},t\}+\Delta. \Delta is known, but the protocol does not know the value of GST. Optimal resiliency in the partial synchrony model means tolerating up to f Byzantine processors among n processors, where f is the largest integer less than n/3.

The view-based paradigm and view synchronization in partial synchrony. Many BFT SMR protocols in the partial synchrony model use a view-based paradigm. The instructions of these protocols are divided into views, and each view has a designated leader that drives progress. During periods of synchrony a consensus decision is guaranteed whenever honest processors spend a long enough time together in some view with an honest leader. The problem of making sure processors synchronize for long enough in the same view is called the Byzantine View Synchronization (BVS) problem.

HotStuff was the first BFT SMR protocol that decoupled the core consensus logic from a “Pacemaker” module that implements BVS, but it did not specify the pacemaker implementation. In HotStuff the core consensus logic needs quadratic communication complexity in the worst case and linear latency, while each view only needs linear complexity and a constant number of rounds. So view synchronization becomes the efficiency bottleneck, and the key question is: Can we design a Byzantine view synchronization protocol with optimal communication complexity and latency?

5. Requirements
- worst-case complexity O(n^{2}) (Dolev-Reischuk bound); o(n^{2}) when f_{a}=o(n)
- worst-case latency O(n\Delta); o(n\Delta) with few faults
- optimistic responsiveness: if f_{a}=0, latency a function of actual delay \delta; O(\delta) after GST
- smoothly optimistically responsive: O(\Delta f_{a}+\delta) for any f_{a}\leq f

6. Prior work and result
- recent works achieve some goals; shortcomings: only benign failures / not optimal worst-case / large cost with few faults / clock synchronization
- Lumiere first BVS protocol in partial synchrony with all properties
- Theorem: (1) O(n^{2}) worst-case communication, (2) O(n\Delta) worst-case latency, (3) smoothly optimistically responsive, (4) eventual O(f_{a}n+n)
- Section 2 definitions; Table 1; Section 6

7. Approach
- combine LP22 and Fever
- LP22: epochs of f+1 views, heavy \Theta(n^{2}) sync at epoch start; one faulty leader -> \Theta(n\Delta) delays
- Fever: optimal but synchronized clocks
- epochs + Fever within epochs -> (1)–(3)
- property (4): stop heavy epoch changes once synchronized; Section 3.5

steps.text:
State machine replication (SMR) is a central topic in distributed computing. It refers to the task of implementing a fault-tolerant service by replicating servers and coordinating the interactions of clients with the server replicas. Partly because of high levels of investment in ‘blockchain’ technology, in recent years there has been interest in developing SMR protocols that work efficiently at scale. Concretely, this means trying to minimize the latency and the communication complexity per consensus decision as a function of the number of processors (participants) n.

SMR protocols usually aim for Byzantine fault tolerance, which means consensus among the processors (server replicas) even if a bounded proportion of them are Byzantine and behave arbitrarily/maliciously. Many of these protocols are based on the partial synchrony model, which is a common networking model and can be seen as a practical compromise between the synchronous and asynchronous communication models. The model assumes a point in time called the global stabilisation time (GST) so that any message sent at time t has to arrive by time \max\{\text{GST},t\}+\Delta. \Delta is known, but the protocol does not know the value of GST. Optimal resiliency in the partial synchrony model means tolerating up to f Byzantine processors among n processors, where f is the largest integer less than n/3.

The view-based paradigm and view synchronization in partial synchrony. Many BFT SMR protocols in the partial synchrony model use a view-based paradigm. The instructions of these protocols are divided into views, and each view has a designated leader that drives progress. During periods of synchrony a consensus decision is guaranteed whenever honest processors spend a long enough time together in some view with an honest leader. The problem of making sure processors synchronize for long enough in the same view is called the Byzantine View Synchronization (BVS) problem.

HotStuff was the first BFT SMR protocol that decoupled the core consensus logic from a “Pacemaker” module that implements BVS, but it did not specify the pacemaker implementation. In HotStuff the core consensus logic needs quadratic communication complexity in the worst case and linear latency, while each view only needs linear complexity and a constant number of rounds. So view synchronization becomes the efficiency bottleneck, and the key question is: Can we design a Byzantine view synchronization protocol with optimal communication complexity and latency?

We need to say more about the communication complexity and latency we want. The worst-case complexity should be O(n^{2}) to meet the Dolev-Reischuk bound. But when there are fewer actual faults f_{a}\leq f, we would like the worst-case complexity between every pair of consensus decisions to be a function of f_{a}, so that the complexity is o(n^{2}) when f_{a}=o(n). In the same way, the worst-case latency is O(n\Delta), but we would like latency o(n\Delta) when there is a small number f_{a} of actual faults. Also, since the core consensus logic can provide optimistic responsiveness, this property would be good to have in BVS too. Roughly, it means the protocol should work at ‘network speed’ if it turns out the actual number of faults f_{a}\leq f is 0: if f_{a}=0, the protocol should be live during periods where message delay is less than the given bound \Delta, and latency should be a function of the actual (unknown) message delay \delta. This matters because the actual message delay \delta can be much smaller than \Delta when \Delta is set conservatively to ensure liveness under a wide range of network conditions. More formally, a protocol is optimistically responsive if, after some finite time after GST, the worst-case latency between synchronized views with honest leaders (each of which will produce a consensus decision) is O(\delta) when f_{a}=0. Generalizing this, a protocol is smoothly optimistically responsive if the corresponding bound is O(\Delta f_{a}+\delta) for any value of f_{a}\leq f.

Recent works have addressed the Byzantine view synchronization problem and achieved some of these goals. But all of them either tolerate only benign failures, or do not get optimal worst-case communication and latency, or need a large communication complexity and latency even when there are only a small number of faults, or need stronger assumptions such as clock synchronization. Lumiere is the first Byzantine view synchronization protocol in the partial synchrony model that achieves all of these properties at the same time. The key result is the following:

Lumiere is a BVS protocol for the partial synchrony model with the following properties:

- (1) Worst-case communication complexity O(n^{2}).

- (2) Worst-case latency O(n\Delta).

- (3) The protocol is smoothly optimistically responsive.

- (4) Eventual worst case communication complexity O(f_{a}n+n).

All the terms in Theorem 1.1 are formally defined in Section 2. Table 1 compares the relevant performance measures for state-of-the-art protocols, and Section 6 describes the comparison in more detail.

We want to emphasize that Lumiere is the first BVS protocol for partial synchrony that satisfies (1) and (2) from Theorem 1.1 and also satisfies either (3) or (4) (in fact it satisfies both). The basic approach to get a protocol that is smoothly optimistically responsive and satisfies properties (1) and (2) is to combine techniques from LP22 and Fever. LP22 gets worst-case communication complexity O(n^{2}) by dividing the instructions into epochs, where each epoch has f+1 views. It performs a heavy (\Theta(n^{2}) communication complexity) synchronization process only once at the start of each epoch, so there is no need for synchronization within epochs, and this matches the Dolev-Reischuk bound. LP22 is also optimistically responsive, but it has the problem that even a single faulty leader can then cause \Theta(n\Delta) delays. Fever, on the other hand, is optimal for all measures we consider in this paper, but it needs synchronized clocks (so it works in a non-standard model). We show that by using epochs (like LP22) and running Fever within epochs, we can get a protocol for the partial synchrony model that satisfies properties (1)–(3) at the same time.

The most technically complex task is then to change the protocol so that the eventual worst case communication complexity is also O(f_{a}n+n) (property (4)). For this we need to establish conditions that let processors stop doing heavy epoch changes once they are sufficiently synchronized. This involves a number of substantial technical complexities, which are discussed in depth in Section 3.5.

View synchronization therefore becomes the efficiency bottleneck, and the key question becomes: Can we design a Byzantine view synchronization protocol with optimal communication complexity and latency?

The desired communication complexity and latency requirements need some elaboration. Worst-case complexity should be O(n^{2}) to meet the Dolev-Reischuk bound [8]. However, when there are fewer actual faults f_{a}\leq f, one would hope for the worst-case complexity between every pair of consensus decisions to be a function of f_{a}, so that complexity is o(n^{2}) when f_{a}=o(n). Likewise, while worst-case latency is O(n\Delta), one would hope for latency o(n\Delta) when there is a small number f_{a} of actual faults. Furthermore, since the core consensus logic can provide optimistic responsiveness, this property would be desirable in BVS as well. Roughly, this means the protocol should run at ‘network speed’ if the actual number of faults f_{a}\leq f turns out to be 0: if f_{a}=0, the protocol should be live during periods when message delay is less than the given bound \Delta, and latency should be a function of the actual (unknown) message delay \delta. This is important because the actual message delay \delta may be much smaller than \Delta when the latter is conservatively set to ensure liveness under a wide range of network conditions. More formally, a protocol is optimistically responsive if, after some finite time after GST, the worst-case latency between synchronized views with honest leaders (each of which will produce a consensus decision) is O(\delta) when f_{a}=0. Generalizing this, a protocol is smoothly optimistically responsive if the corresponding bound is O(\Delta f_{a}+\delta) for any value of f_{a}\leq f.

Recent works have addressed the Byzantine view synchronization problem and achieved some of the goals described above [9,10,11,12,13]. However, all of those works either tolerate only benign failures [9], do not obtain optimal worst-case communication and latency [10], require large communication complexity and latency even when there are few faults [11,12,13], or require stronger assumptions such as clock synchronization [14]. Lumiere is the first Byzantine view synchronization protocol in the partial synchrony model to achieve all of these properties simultaneously. The key result is the following:

Lumiere is a BVS protocol for the partial synchrony model with the following properties:

- (1) Worst-case communication complexity O(n^{2}).

- (2) Worst-case latency O(n\Delta).

- (3) The protocol is smoothly optimistically responsive.

- (4) Eventual worst case communication complexity O(f_{a}n+n).

All terms in Theorem 1.1 are formally defined in Section 2. Table 1 compares the relevant performance measures for state-of-the-art protocols; the comparison is described in more detail in Section 6.

We emphasize that Lumiere is the first BVS protocol for partial synchrony that satisfies (1) and (2) from Theorem 1.1 while also satisfying either (3) or (4) (in fact, it satisfies both). The basic approach to obtaining a protocol that is smoothly optimistically responsive while satisfying properties (1) and (2) is to combine techniques from LP22 [11] and Fever [14]. LP22 achieves worst-case communication complexity O(n^{2}) by dividing the instructions into epochs, each consisting of f+1 views. By performing a heavy (\Theta(n^{2}) communication complexity) synchronization process only once at the beginning of each epoch, it avoids the need for synchronization within epochs and thereby matches the Dolev-Reischuk bound [8]. LP22 also achieves optimistic responsiveness, but suffers from the issue that even a single faulty leader can cause \Theta(n\Delta) delays. Fever, meanwhile, is optimal for all measures considered in this paper, but requires synchronized clocks (and so operates in a non-standard model). We show that by using epochs (as in LP22) and employing Fever within epochs, one can obtain a protocol for the partial synchrony model that simultaneously satisfies properties (1)–(3).

The most technically complex task is then to modify the protocol so that the eventual worst case communication complexity is also O(f_{a}n+n) (property (4)). This requires establishing conditions that allow processors to stop carrying out heavy epoch changes once sufficiently synchronized, which involves a number of substantial technical complexities discussed in depth in Section 3.5.
